comments.selected: Gull Terrace ran along the top of the town in a crescent of

block.text: Gull Terrace ran along the top of the town in a crescent of stubborn houses, all of them facing the sea like a jury. Number nine had her father's brass plate still on the door — E. VANE, MASTER PILOT — burnished by eleven years of nobody's thumb. The key stuck, as it had always stuck, in the particular way that had once driven her mother to oil it with butter and her father to declare the lock a better judge of character than the church. It gave at last with a sound like a small, private thunderclap, and the house received her in a gust of cold, still air that smelled of dust, lavender gone to seed, and — absurdly, unforgivably — of the turpentine and lamp oil of the chart room, as if the place had been keeping its own counsel in its own smells, waiting.

comments.selected: The walk down to the harbour took her past everything the to

block.text: The walk down to the harbour took her past everything the town had preserved in her absence and everything it had let fall. The chapel had a new roof and an old congregation. The inn had a new landlord, who was the old landlord's daughter, and a sign — THE KEEPER'S ARMS, repainted, the painted ship on it still steering, as it had steered all Mara's childhood, confidently toward a painted rock. The chart agent's shop, where her father's corrections had once been sold in a rack by the door, sold postcards now, and fishing tackle, and in the window a pyramid of the official chart of Gullwick and Approaches in its blue Admiralty wrapper — her chart, her chart. She stood looking at it longer than the postcards warranted. Nothing on it was hers yet. The approaches it showed were the approaches of her whole professional life: competent, elegant, and — in one six-inch square east of the beacon — a beautiful, authoritative, well-drafted lie, with her own profession's imprimatur in the corner.

comments.selected: Mr. Venn spoke first, for the underwriters, and he was — Mar

block.text: Mr. Venn spoke first, for the underwriters, and he was — Mara would grant him this in every retelling for the rest of her life — magnificent. He did not defend the lie. He conceded the soundings in a sentence, the ledger in a clause, the Cormorant in a silence he allowed to stand exactly long enough to be priced. He spoke instead of order. A channel, gentlemen, is not a fact; it is an institution. Print it raw upon the world's charts and you do not liberate the water, you abandon it — to every under-insured tramp and holiday admiral who can read a blue line and cannot read a tide; to insurers who will raise the port's premiums past bearing; to a harbour whose pilotage, the town's second income, becomes worthless in a season; to the men in this room, whose fathers' knowledge, held in trust, will be given away by a woman who has been absent eleven years and will, if history is any guide, be absent again by winter. "The Keeper," he said, "proposes generosity with other men's inheritance. The firm proposes prudence with everyone's. We will buy the survey — at the price already offered, doubled — and hold it, and release it in order, in season, through the Board, as pilots are trained to it. That is not suppression, gentlemen. That is seamanship, applied to information."

comment.quote: Mr. Venn spoke first, for the underwriters, and he was — Mar
comment.body: [sim] comment 6 from sim05 on sim06's draft
